Ears and eyes are what you would ask of a monarch: attention, a hearing, notice taken. A man drafting a petition asks to be seen and heard, because that is as much as he can decently request. Nobody asks a king for his heart.

God volunteers it. He will not merely monitor the building; his affection will be lodged in it. And the phrase he uses of the house — my name, my eyes, my heart — is the language of a man describing where he has left something precious. Solomon asked for surveillance and was given attachment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — The Epitaph, Written in Advance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word turns personal: if you will walk before me as David your father walked, the throne will stand and you shall not lack a man to rule Israel (vv. 17-18). But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes ... and go and serve other gods (v. 19), then I will pluck you up from my land ... and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight (v. 20). Passers-by will ask why (v. 21), and God supplies the answer they will give: because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: On the day the temple is dedicated God describes its ruin and writes the inscription for it. Four hundred years later the last chapter of this book reports the burning and gives the same reason in almost the same words.
verseByVerse.examples: The verb in verse 22 is the one that runs through the whole book. They abandoned him — the same word Azariah will put to Asa, and Zechariah to Joash, and the Chronicler to Judah at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to rule Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word now turns from the house to the man. And as for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne.

The standard held up to him is his father, and precision matters about what that means, because David's record is in this book and it includes a census that killed seventy thousand people. The measure is not a clean life. It is the direction of one: a man who sought God, got it wrong, was told, said I have sinned greatly without being asked twice, and went and found out how to do it properly.

And the promise attached is the one from Nathan's night: you shall not lack a man to rule Israel. Solomon had quoted it in his prayer with the condition attached, and God repeats it to him with the condition attached, so that nobody can say afterwards that it was not made clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you, and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples. And at this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by will be astonished and say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?' Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore he has brought all this disaster on them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, at the end of the greatest day in the history of Israel, God describes the ruin.

But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you, and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight.

Notice my land. Not your land, which you may forfeit — mine, which I gave you. The tenancy language runs all the way through both these books: the throne is the LORD's, and so is the ground, and so is the house he has just filled with fire and smoke.

And the house is not spared in the sentence. God says he will cast out of his sight the building he has consecrated for his name, four hours after consecrating it, and make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples.

Then he writes the inscription. And at this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by will be astonished and say, Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house? Then they will say, Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods.

God supplies both halves of the exchange — the traveller's question and the answer he will be given. On the day of the dedication the epitaph is already cut.

Four hundred years later the last chapter of this book reports what happened, and it uses the same reasoning almost word for word: they kept mocking the messengers of God until there was no remedy, and the Chaldeans burned the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem. Nobody who had this chapter could say they had not been told.

So the high point of the book contains its ending, and the promise and the warning stand in the same paragraph, spoken the same night, by the same voice. The house that could be cast out of his sight was never the thing that would last. What lasts is in verse 14, and it does not require a building — four verbs from a people over whom his name is called, and three from a God who hears, forgives and heals.

8.title: All That Solomon Planned to Do
8.text: <sup>1</sup>At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house,<sup>2</sup>Solomon rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to him, and settled the people of Israel in them.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and took it.<sup>4</sup>He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath.<sup>5</sup>He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars,<sup>6</sup>and Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had and all the cities for his chariots and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.<sup>7</sup>All the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel,<sup>8</sup>from their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel had not destroyed—these Solomon drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day.<sup>9</sup>But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were soldiers, and his officers, the commanders of his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>10</sup>And these were the chief officers of King Solomon, 250, who exercised authority over the people.<sup>11</sup>Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the city of David to the house that he had built for her, for he said, "My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy."<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon offered up burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD that he had built before the vestibule,<sup>13</sup>as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual feasts—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths.<sup>14</sup>According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded.<sup>15</sup>And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded the priests and Levites concerning any matter and concerning the treasuries.<sup>16</sup>Thus was accomplished all the work of Solomon from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was completed.<sup>17</sup>Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the sea, in the land of Edom.<sup>18</sup>And Hiram sent to him by the hand of his servants ships and servants familiar with the sea, and they went to Ophir together with the servants of Solomon and brought from there 450 talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon.
8.overview:
Twenty years of building are summarised: cities rebuilt, Hamath-zobah taken, Tadmor and the store cities raised, Beth-horon fortified (vv. 1-6). The Canaanite remnant is drafted as forced labour while no Israelite is enslaved (vv. 7-10), and Pharaoh's daughter is moved out of David's house on grounds of holiness (v. 11). Then the worship is established — what is offered according to Moses, who offers it according to David — and nobody turns aside from it (vv. 12-16). The chapter closes with a Phoenician-crewed fleet returning from Ophir with 450 talents of gold (vv. 17-18).

Verse 11 is the nearest this book comes to Solomon's foreign marriages. There is no eleventh chapter of Kings here: the wives, the high places for Chemosh and Molech, and the tearing of the kingdom are all absent.
8.theology:
Verses 13 and 14 name two authorities in consecutive sentences and rank neither. The commandment of Moses governs what is offered and when; the ruling of David governs who does it — and David is given the title Scripture uses of Moses, the man of God. The law and the arrangement are not rivals. One was revealed and the other was devised in obedience to it, and the Chronicler treats both as binding.

And verse 11 shows what devotion looks like when it is applied at the wrong point. Solomon reasons carefully about which house his Egyptian wife may live in, on grounds of holiness, and the law he is being careful about had forbidden the marriage itself. Precision in a small matter is no protection at all when the large one has already been conceded.
8.examples:
He walled Upper and Lower Beth-horon. A woman named Sheerah had founded those two towns generations before, and the richest king in the nation's history built on ground somebody else had chosen.

Verse 15 records that nobody turned aside from the rotas. A generation after the lots were drawn the men were still arriving in the right week and the treasuries were still being accounted for — which is harder than building the house, and far less interesting to write about.

Israel could not sail, so Solomon hired men who could and sent his own along with them. The same instinct that had asked Tyre for woodsmen put Phoenician crews on Israelite ships.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Twenty Years, and What He Built
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house (v. 1), the record turns to everything else: cities rebuilt and settled (v. 2), Hamath-zobah taken, Tadmor and the store cities built (vv. 3-4), Upper and Lower Beth-horon fortified with walls, gates, and bars, and the chariot cities — whatever Solomon desired to build (vv. 5-6). The Canaanite remnant is drafted as forced labour, but of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work (vv. 7-10). And Pharaoh's daughter is moved out of David's house, because the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 11 is the only place the Chronicler lets us hear Solomon reason about his Egyptian wife, and what he reasons about is her address. Where she may live is settled on grounds of holiness. Whether he should have married her is a question this book never raises.
verseByVerse.examples: He fortified Upper and Lower Beth-horon. A woman called Sheerah built those two towns generations earlier — the only person in nine chapters of genealogy credited with putting up anything at all — and the richest king in Israel's history walled what she had founded.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house, Solomon rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to him, and settled the people of Israel in them. And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and took it. He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath. He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars, and Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had and all the cities for his chariots and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own house.

Twenty years for the two of them. The other account divides the total: seven on God's house and thirteen on his own. Chronicles gives the sum and moves on, and does not do the subtraction for anybody.

Then verse 2, which reads oddly against the other account: Solomon rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to him. In Kings the traffic runs the other way — Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, and Hiram goes out to inspect them and is unimpressed and calls the whole district Cabul, which means about as much as good-for-nothing. The likeliest explanation is that he handed them back, and that Chronicles is describing what Solomon did with them afterwards. It cannot be proved, and nothing turns on it.

Then the building list, and it is the list of a man securing a trade empire: Tadmor out in the desert on the caravan road, store cities in Hamath, the chariot cities, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.

One entry deserves a second look. He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars. Those two towns already existed, and the register in the earlier book says who founded them: Sheerah, a daughter of Ephraim, the one person in nine chapters of genealogy credited with building anything at all. She put them on the ridge that guards the pass up from the coastal plain. Centuries later the wealthiest king Israel ever had walls what she started, because she had chosen the right hill.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel, from their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel had not destroyed—these Solomon drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day. But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were soldiers, and his officers, the commanders of his chariots, and his horsemen. And these were the chief officers of King Solomon, 250, who exercised authority over the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The labour question is answered directly, and the Chronicler does not soften either half.

The Canaanite remnant — Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites, the peoples Israel had not driven out — these Solomon drafted as forced labor, and so they are to this day. It is conscription of a subject population, described without apology, and the phrase at the end tells us the arrangement was still running when the source was written.

But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were soldiers, and his officers, the commanders of his chariots, and his horsemen.

Two classes of person under one crown, and the line between them is ethnic. Israelites commanded; the residents who were not Israelites carried. The Chronicler states it as a fact of the reign rather than as a policy he is defending.

There is a difficulty here, and it should be named. The book of Kings says Solomon raised a levy of thirty thousand men out of all Israel and sent them to Lebanon in shifts. The usual reading is that this was a rotating obligation of a few months rather than the permanent servitude the Canaanites were put under, and that the two accounts are describing different things. The reader who is troubled by it is not being unreasonable, and should know that a generation later the northern tribes will name forced labour as their grievance and that the man in charge of it will be stoned to death on the road.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the city of David to the house that he had built for her, for he said, "My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon brought Pharaoh's daughter up from the city of David to the house that he had built for her, for he said, My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy.

Kings records the move in half a sentence. Chronicles gives the reasoning, and the reasoning is scrupulous. The ark has been in that quarter of the city; ground the ark has occupied is holy; his Egyptian wife will therefore live somewhere else, in a house built for her. He has thought about it carefully and he has thought about it wrongly, and the Chronicler sets it down without a syllable of comment.

Because the question the verse raises is not where she should live. Israel's law had said plainly that a king was not to make marriages with the surrounding nations, and had given the reason: they will turn away your sons from following me. The precise, devout, geographical care in this verse is being exercised about a marriage that should not have existed.

And here we come to the largest thing this book leaves out. There is no eleventh chapter of Kings in Chronicles. The seven hundred wives and the three hundred concubines are not here. The high places built on the hill east of Jerusalem for Chemosh and Molech are not here. God's anger, and the sentence that the kingdom would be torn away, are not here. The Chronicler ends Solomon's reign with him sleeping with his fathers and says nothing at all.

He does not conceal it, any more than he concealed what David did to Uriah while omitting the story. In the next chapter he will name the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite concerning Jeroboam, and when the kingdom splits he will say the division was a turn of affairs brought about by God to fulfil that word — and any reader who wants to know why Ahijah said it has to open the other book. The door is left standing open. He simply walks past it.

What he gives instead is Solomon at his best, because his subject is the temple and the throne rather than the man. And this verse is what that looks like from the inside: a king being meticulous about holiness in the one place where meticulousness could not help him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — According to Moses, According to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worship is set running and two authorities are named for it. The offerings go up as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for Sabbaths, new moons and the three annual feasts (vv. 12-13). The staffing follows the ruling of David his father — the divisions of priests, the Levites in their offices of praise, the gatekeepers at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded (v. 14). And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded (v. 15). The work is declared complete (v. 16), and the fleet sails from Ezion-geber to Ophir and brings back 450 talents of gold (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses commanded what was offered; David arranged who did it and when. The Chronicler puts the two names in consecutive verses without ranking them, and calls David by a title otherwise reserved for Moses — the man of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is the quiet triumph of the whole arrangement. The rotas drawn by lot in front of David and Zadok were still being kept a generation later, and nobody had drifted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon offered up burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD that he had built before the vestibule, as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual feasts—the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths. According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded. And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded the priests and Levites concerning any matter and concerning the treasuries. Thus was accomplished all the work of Solomon from the day the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid until it was finished. So the house of the LORD was completed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the worship is set going, and two names are given for how it is done.

First: the offerings go up on the altar as the duty of each day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual feasts. What is offered, and when, comes from the law. Nothing here is Solomon's invention.

Then: According to the ruling of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their offices of praise and ministry ... and the gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate, for so David the man of God had commanded.

The rotas are David's. Twenty-four courses of priests, twenty-four of singers, the doorkeepers drawn by lot small and great alike — all of it set up by an old man in his last years for a building he never entered, and all of it running.

And note the title attached to him: David the man of God. That is what Scripture calls Moses. The Chronicler puts the two names in consecutive verses, gives each his own domain — Moses says what is offered, David says who does it and when — and declines to rank them.

Then verse 15, which is a small sentence about a large achievement. And they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded the priests and Levites concerning any matter and concerning the treasuries.

Nobody drifted. A generation after the lots were drawn, the men were still turning up in the right week and the accounts were still being kept. That is harder than building the house and less interesting to write about, and it is why the Chronicler mentions it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent to him by the hand of his servants ships and servants familiar with the sea, and they went to Ophir together with the servants of Solomon and brought from there 450 talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends at sea. Solomon goes down to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the gulf, in Edomite territory, and Hiram sends him ships and servants familiar with the sea.

Israel was not a maritime people. It had a coastline it did not control and no tradition of deep-water sailing, and the arrangement here is the same one as the timber: the Phoenicians knew how, and Solomon hired them and sent his own men along to learn.

They come back from Ophir with four hundred and fifty talents of gold — the account in Kings says four hundred and twenty, and no one can account for the difference. Either way it is an enormous sum arriving in a single voyage, and the next chapter is about what happens to a kingdom when gold starts coming in faster than anybody can count it.

9.title: Something Greater Than Solomon Is Here
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions, having a very great retinue and camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her.<sup>3</sup>And when the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,<sup>4</sup>the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, and their clothing, his cupbearers, and their clothing, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.<sup>5</sup>And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom,<sup>6</sup>but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, half the greatness of your wisdom was not told me; you surpass the report that I heard.<sup>7</sup>Happy are your men! Happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!<sup>8</sup>Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness."<sup>9</sup>Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There were no spices such as those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.<sup>10</sup>Moreover, the servants of Hiram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood and precious stones.<sup>11</sup>And the king made from the algum wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, lyres also and harps for the singers. There never was seen the like of them before in the land of Judah.<sup>12</sup>And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what she had brought to the king. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.<sup>13</sup>Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold,<sup>14</sup>besides that which the explorers and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought gold and silver to Solomon.<sup>15</sup>King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of beaten gold went into each shield.<sup>16</sup>And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; 300 shekels of gold went into each shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.<sup>17</sup>The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold.<sup>18</sup>The throne had six steps and a footstool of gold, which were attached to the throne, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests,<sup>19</sup>while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. Nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom.<sup>20</sup>All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon.<sup>21</sup>For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Hiram. Once every three years the ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.<sup>22</sup>Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.<sup>23</sup>And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind.<sup>24</sup>Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and of gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.<sup>25</sup>And Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>And he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.<sup>27</sup>And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>28</sup>And horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.<sup>29</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?<sup>30</sup>Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.<sup>31</sup>And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
9.overview:
The queen of Sheba arrives to test Solomon with riddles, is answered, and is left breathless by what she sees — ending the list with his burnt offerings at the house of the LORD (vv. 1-4). Her speech concedes the reports were understated, envies his servants, and blesses Israel's God in terms most Israelites never managed (vv. 5-8). Gifts are exchanged and she goes home with all she asked for (vv. 9-12). Then the wealth: 666 talents a year, five hundred gold shields, an ivory throne with fourteen lions, silver counted as nothing, and a fleet bringing apes and peacocks (vv. 13-21). The reign is summed up (vv. 22-24) and closes with the same stables and the same Egyptian horses it opened with (vv. 25-28); the sources are filed and Solomon is buried (vv. 29-31).

Two of the three sources named in verse 29 are about Jeroboam — the man who will take ten tribes from Solomon's son. The Chronicler files them and does not tell the story.
9.theology:
The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 forbids three accumulations: horses, and Egypt as their source; wives; and excessive silver and gold. Chapter 1 ended on the first. The second is in the book this one declines to quote. This chapter is the third, reported as splendour, with the figures given. The Chronicler makes no accusation and assumes his reader has Deuteronomy — and the reign that opened with Egyptian horses closes, forty years later, in the same words.

Against that stands verse 8, where a foreign queen states Israel's monarchy correctly: God's own throne, occupied on God's behalf, given because God loved the people, so that justice and righteousness might be done. Hiram had said the same thing in a letter seven chapters ago. Twice in this book the doctrine of the throne is put most clearly by outsiders.
9.examples:
What took the queen's breath was last on the list. She had already seen the house, the table, the officials, the servants and the liveries; what emptied her lungs was watching the king go up and burn things at the house of the LORD.

She envied the staff rather than the king — happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom. The people nearest a good thing are usually the last to notice they have it.

Five hundred shields of beaten gold, hung in a hall built to display them. Within one reign they were carried off by an Egyptian army and replaced with bronze copies that had to be kept under guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She comes to test him with hard questions with camels carrying spices and gold, and tells him everything on her mind; there was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her (vv. 1-2). Then she looks: the wisdom, the house, the food, the seating of his officials, the servants and their clothing, the cupbearers — and his burnt offerings at the house of the LORD — there was no more breath in her (vv. 3-4). Her speech admits the report was true and the half had not been told (vv. 5-7), and ends by blessing Israel's God (v. 8). She gives 120 talents of gold and spices such as had never been seen (vv. 9-11), and Solomon gives her all that she desired (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing on the list that took her breath away is not the food or the furniture. It is the burnt offerings he offered at the house of the LORD. She had come to test a reputation for cleverness and what finished her was watching him worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is the second time in this book that a foreign monarch has blessed the LORD and described Israel's throne better than most Israelites did — God's own throne, occupied for God, because God loved the people, so that justice and righteousness could be done.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions, having a very great retinue and camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her. And when the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, and their clothing, his cupbearers, and their clothing, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She comes a very long way. Sheba is in the south-west of Arabia, fifteen hundred miles off, and she arrives with a caravan of camels because there is no other way to cross that distance — and she comes to test him with hard questions.

The word is the one used for riddles. This is a formal contest of the kind monarchs held: you put your hardest problems to a rival court and see whether they can be answered. She has come to find out whether the reports are exaggerated, which is what an intelligent ruler does with a reputation.

And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing hidden from Solomon that he could not explain to her.

Then she stops asking and starts looking, and the Chronicler gives the list in the order she saw it: the wisdom, the house he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, the attendance of his servants and their clothing, his cupbearers and their clothing — and then one more item.

And his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.

The last thing on the list is worship, and it is the last thing on the list because that is where the sentence breaks. She had absorbed the architecture and the catering and the livery. What emptied her lungs was watching the king go up to the house of God and give things away by the thousand.

A wealthy woman who had come to test a clever man ends the inspection winded, and the thing that did it was not what Solomon had but what he burned.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, half the greatness of your wisdom was not told me; you surpass the report that I heard. Happy are your men! Happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take her speech slowly, because she gets more right than most of Israel did.

She begins by conceding: the report was true that I heard in my own land — and then admits she had not believed it. I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, half the greatness of your wisdom was not told me. She had come to catch out an exaggeration and found an understatement.

Then she envies the staff. Happy are your men! Happy are these your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Not happy is the king — happy are the people who get to stand in the room every day and listen. She has understood that proximity to wisdom is the privilege, and that the courtiers who take it for granted have the best of it.

And then verse 8, which is the reason this speech is in Scripture.

Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on his throne as king for the LORD your God! Because your God loved Israel and would establish them forever, he has made you king over them, that you may execute justice and righteousness.

Take it clause by clause. His throne — not Solomon's; the chair belongs to God, which is what the previous book said three times and what Solomon's own father told the assembly. As king for the LORD — he holds it on someone else's behalf. Because your God loved Israel — the king exists because of God's affection for the people, which is precisely what Hiram of Tyre wrote in his letter and what the Chronicler said when the first cedar arrived in David's Jerusalem. And that you may execute justice and righteousness — the pair that measured David and will measure every king after him.

A pagan queen from the far end of Arabia has just stated the theology of Israel's monarchy in one sentence, and she is the second foreigner in this book to do it. The Chronicler's readers, living under a Persian governor and wondering whether their God was known outside their own province, are being handed something.

Centuries later a man from Nazareth told a crowd that the queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and that something greater than Solomon was standing in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There were no spices such as those that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Moreover, the servants of Hiram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood and precious stones. And the king made from the algum wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, lyres also and harps for the singers. There never was seen the like of them before in the land of Judah. And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what she had brought to the king. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gifts are enormous — a hundred and twenty talents of gold, and spices in a quantity the writer says was never matched. Trade between Jerusalem and southern Arabia is being opened, and both parties know it.

Then a detail slipped in from the fleet: the ships from Ophir also brought algum wood, and Solomon made from it supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, lyres also and harps for the singers.

Exotic timber from the far side of the world, and what he does with it is make instruments for the choir. The trade empire feeds the music of the temple. His father had made instruments with his own hands for the same purpose; the son buys the wood by the shipload.

And the queen goes home with all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what she had brought to the king. She gave a great deal and received more, and she asked for whatever she wanted and got it — which is exactly what Solomon had prayed at the dedication that God would do for any foreigner who came from a far country toward this house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Gold, and the Law of the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The annual revenue is given as 666 talents of gold, besides that which the explorers and merchants brought, with the kings of Arabia and the governors adding more (vv. 13-14). Five hundred shields of beaten gold are made and hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (vv. 15-16). A great ivory throne overlaid with gold is built, with six steps and twelve lions — nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom (vv. 17-19). Every drinking vessel is gold, and silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon (v. 20), the fleet returning every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The law of the king in Deuteronomy named three things a king was not to accumulate: horses, wives, and excessive silver and gold. Chapter 1 showed the first, this chapter shows the third, and the second is in the book this one does not quote.
verseByVerse.examples: Five hundred gold shields hang in a hall built for them. Three chapters from now an Egyptian army will carry every one of them away, and Rehoboam will have replicas made in bronze and put a guard on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which the explorers and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought gold and silver to Solomon. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of beaten gold went into each shield. And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; 300 shekels of gold went into each shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which the explorers and merchants brought.

Twenty-five tons, in a year, before trade income. Readers have long noticed the number and there is no need to make anything of it; the point the Chronicler's own Bible makes lies somewhere else.

Turn back to the law of the king in Deuteronomy. Three things a king of Israel was not to accumulate: he shall not multiply horses, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to get them; he shall not multiply wives, lest his heart turn away; and he shall not greatly multiply for himself silver and gold.

Chapter 1 of this book ended with the horses, imported from Egypt, in the same breath as the promise of riches being kept. The wives are in the book this one does not quote. And here, in the closing chapter of the reign, is the third — reported as splendour, with the figures.

The Chronicler does not editorialise. He is writing the glory of Solomon and this is part of it, and he assumes his reader has Deuteronomy. What he shows is a man who received wisdom as a gift, and prosperity as a bonus he had not asked for, and then spent forty years accumulating in three of the exact categories the law had marked out.

The gold goes into shields. Five hundred of them, beaten gold, two hundred large and three hundred smaller, hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. They are ceremonial — gold is soft and no one fights with it — and they exist to be looked at.

Keep them in view. Three chapters from now, in the fifth year of Solomon's son, an Egyptian army will walk into Jerusalem and take every one of them, and Rehoboam will have copies made in bronze and hand them to the guard.

verseByVerse.quote: The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold. The throne had six steps and a footstool of gold, which were attached to the throne, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests, while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. Nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom. All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. For the king's ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Hiram. Once every three years the ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the throne, described in more detail than anything else Solomon owned. Ivory overlaid with pure gold. Six steps up to it, with a golden footstool attached. Armrests with a lion standing on either side, and twelve more lions, one at each end of each step.

Nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom.

Fourteen lions and a man climbing six steps to sit above them. The lion is Judah's animal — the lion's cub who does not let the sceptre depart — and the arrangement says what a throne room is for: everyone who came in had to look up.

Then the drinking vessels, all of gold, and a sentence that measures the reign better than any total: Silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. Silver, which every other nation in the region used as money, was beneath notice in Jerusalem.

And the fleet comes in once every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. The last two items are worth a moment. Apes and peacocks are not commodities. Nobody eats them, builds with them or trades on them. They are curiosities for a court that already has everything, which is what happens at the far end of a supply chain when there is nothing left to want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — The Reign Ends Where It Began
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom (v. 22), and they came to hear the wisdom which God had put into his mind, bringing tribute year by year (vv. 23-24). Then the stables: four thousand stalls, twelve thousand horsemen (v. 25); dominion from the Euphrates to Egypt (v. 26); silver as common as stone (v. 27); and horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands (v. 28). The sources are named — Nathan, Ahijah the Shilonite, Iddo the seer (v. 29) — and forty years end with a burial and a successor (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 puts riches before wisdom. At Gibeon the order was the other way round: wisdom granted, riches added. Nobody says the wisdom has gone, and the sentence has quietly changed shape.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's death got a paragraph explaining why he died. David's got a good old age, full of days, riches and honour. Solomon gets forty years, a grave and the name of his son.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom. And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind. Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and of gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.

Read the order. At Gibeon, God had said: wisdom and knowledge are granted to you, and I will also give you riches. Wisdom first, riches added. Here the summary of the reign puts riches first and wisdom second.

Nothing in the sentence says the wisdom is gone. The Chronicler makes no accusation and the words could be read as simple sequence. But it is the same two nouns God used, and they have swapped places, and the man who once told God he had not asked for possessions or wealth or honour is now being summed up by them.

And the kings come. All the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind — the writer will not let the wisdom be Solomon's own achievement even in a verse about his fame — and every one of them brings tribute, year by year: silver, gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses and mules.

Horses. In the tribute list, arriving annually, from everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign now ends where it began, and the Chronicler does not appear to arrange it. He simply reports the same facts in the same words.

Chapter 1 closed with fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem; silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stone; cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah; and horses imported from Egypt.

Chapter 9 closes with four thousand stalls and twelve thousand horsemen stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem; silver as common in Jerusalem as stone; cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah; and horses were imported for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.

Forty years between the two paragraphs, and they are the same paragraph. Whatever else happened in that time — a temple built and filled with fire, the wisest man alive answering a queen's riddles, tribute from every court in the region — the horses came from Egypt at the start and they were still coming from Egypt at the end.

In between sits verse 26: he ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. That is the territory God described to Abraham. Israel held it once, under this man, and never again.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat? Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sources are named, and one of them has a door in it.

Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are they not written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?

Three prophets again, as at the end of David's reign. But look at the second and third names. Ahijah the Shilonite is the prophet who met Jeroboam on a road outside Jerusalem, tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and told him to take ten of them — and who gave, as the reason, that Solomon had forsaken God and bowed down to Ashtoreth and Chemosh and Milcom. Iddo's visions are said to concern Jeroboam by name.

So the Chronicler knows. He has just written nine chapters about a king at his best without a word of the collapse, and then he files his sources and two of them are about the man who is going to take ten tribes off Solomon's son. He does not tell the story. He tells you where it is written down.

Then the end of the reign, in two sentences. Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.

No verdict. This book gave Saul an obituary that explained his death — he broke faith and did not seek the LORD, and God put him to death. It gave David a good old age, full of days and riches and honour. Solomon gets a number, a grave and a successor, and the writer who assessed the other two says nothing at all about the man who built the temple.

The silence is not neutral and it is not an attack. It is what a careful historian does when the full account is in another book and the reader can go and read it. The house stands, the fire fell, the promise of chapter 7 has been given with its condition attached — and the man is buried without a word said over him.

10.title: The Folly of Rehoboam
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.<sup>2</sup>And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt.<sup>3</sup>And they sent and called him. And Jeroboam and all Israel came and said to Rehoboam,<sup>4</sup>"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Come to me again in three days." So the people went away.<sup>6</sup>Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?"<sup>7</sup>And they said to him, "If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever."<sup>8</sup>But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?"<sup>10</sup>And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to the people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us'; thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs.<sup>11</sup>And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"<sup>12</sup>So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day."<sup>13</sup>And the king answered them harshly; and forsaking the counsel of the old men,<sup>14</sup>King Rehoboam spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."<sup>15</sup>So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>16</sup>And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Each of you to your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So all Israel went to their tents.<sup>17</sup>But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah.<sup>18</sup>Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and the people of Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.
10.overview:
Rehoboam goes north to Shechem to be made king, and Jeroboam returns from Egypt for the occasion (vv. 1-3). The tribes offer to serve if the labour levy is eased (v. 4). The old men who had served Solomon advise him to give way and be served forever; he abandons their counsel for the slogan his contemporaries supply (vv. 5-11). He answers harshly, and the Chronicler adds that it was a turn of affairs brought about by God to fulfil Ahijah's word (vv. 12-15). Israel walks out on an old rebel's slogan, the taskmaster of the forced labour is stoned, and the king flees to Jerusalem by chariot (vv. 16-19).

The grievance is the one this book set up in chapters 2 and 8. The words the tribes leave on are the words of Sheba's revolt, remembered for two generations and ready when a king gave them an occasion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam goes north to Shechem because that is where all Israel had come ... to make him king (v. 1), and Jeroboam comes back from Egypt for it (vv. 2-3). The demand is specific: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father ... and we will serve you (v. 4). Given three days, the king asks the old men who had served Solomon, and they tell him to be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever (vv. 5-7). But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and asked the men he had grown up with, who supplied a slogan about little fingers and scorpions (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The old men's advice is one sentence and it is about serving. Be good to them, please them, speak well to them — and they will serve you forever. The way to be obeyed is to go first, and it was said to a king by men who had watched a kingdom run for forty years.
verseByVerse.examples: The verb in verse 8 is the word this book uses for forsaking God. Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men, and the Chronicler reached for that particular verb to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt. And they sent and called him. And Jeroboam and all Israel came and said to Rehoboam, "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.

He went to them. The coronation is not in Jerusalem, where the temple is and the throne is and his father was buried; it is forty miles north, in the hill country of Ephraim, because that is where the northern tribes have assembled and they have not offered to travel.

Shechem has a history. It is where Joshua gathered all the tribes at the end of his life and told them to choose that day whom they would serve, and set up a great stone under an oak as a witness. It is also where Abimelech had himself made king after killing seventy of his brothers on one stone. Israel has made decisions about who rules it on that ground before, and they have gone both ways.

Jeroboam comes back for it. The Chronicler tells us he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon, and never once says why — the reader who wants the reason has to go to the other book, where a prophet tore a cloak into twelve pieces on a road and gave him ten of them, and Solomon tried to have him killed.

Then the demand, and it is not a demand for independence. Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you.

They are offering to serve. The condition is the labour levy — the carrying and quarrying and timber-hauling that built the temple and the palace and the store cities and the chariot towns. This book has been careful to say that Israelites were not made slaves, and the men standing at Shechem plainly experienced the arrangement differently. They will serve, they say, if the weight comes down.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Come to me again in three days." So the people went away. Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?" And they said to him, "If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever." But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him. And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?" And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to the people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us'; thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks for three days, which is sensible, and then does something better: he asks the men who had stood in front of his father.

Their answer is one sentence, and every verb in it is about giving way. If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever.

Be good to them. Please them. Speak good words. Then they will serve you — and the word at the end is forever. These are men who watched a kingdom run for four decades, and what they have learned is that authority is not held by asserting it. Go first, and you will be followed for the rest of your life.

But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him.

Stop on that verb. It is the word this book uses when Israel forsakes the LORD — the one God himself used at the dedication, when he said the passers-by would ask why the house was in ruins and be told it was because they abandoned the LORD. The Chronicler picks that verb up and applies it to a young man walking out of a room full of grey heads. Forsaking has a smaller form, and it looks like this.

So he asks the men he grew up with — and one word changes between the two consultations. To the old men he had said: how do you advise me to answer this people? To his contemporaries he says: what do you advise that we answer this people?

Me, and then we. In the first room he was a king asking for counsel; in the second he has joined the committee. He is not weighing what they say against what the old men said. He has changed sides, and the pronoun gives him away before anybody has spoken.

And what they give him is not advice. It is a slogan. My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. Then a threat with a sting in the tail: whips for scorpions — either a worse kind of lash or a genuine multiplication of cruelty, and either way an escalation offered as strategy.

Notice what the young men do not do. They do not weigh the grievance, ask whether the levy could be reduced, or consider what the north might do. They tell the king what he will enjoy saying. That is the whole service they render, and he takes it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Each of You to Your Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the third day the king answers harshly, in the young men's words: My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions (vv. 12-14). And the Chronicler names a second cause — it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite (v. 15). Israel answers with an old rebel's slogan: What portion have we in David? ... Each of you to your tents, O Israel! (v. 16). Rehoboam is left with Judah (v. 17), sends the taskmaster of the forced labour, who is stoned to death, and flees to Jerusalem by chariot (v. 18). So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 puts two causes behind one event, as this history did over David's census. A young king's contempt tore the nation in half, and it was a turn of affairs brought about by God to keep a word he had spoken. Neither statement cancels the other, and nobody excuses Rehoboam.
verseByVerse.examples: Told that the yoke was too heavy, he sent the man in charge of the forced labour. It is hard to think of a worse answer, and the crowd stoned him on the road.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day." And the king answered them harshly; and forsaking the counsel of the old men, King Rehoboam spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions." So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days later the assembly comes back and the king answered them harshly, and the Chronicler repeats the whole slogan so that the reader hears it twice: the heavier yoke, the whips, the scorpions.

He also repeats the verb. Forsaking the counsel of the old men — said again, in case it was missed.

Then verse 15, and it is the theological hinge of the chapter.

So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God that the LORD might fulfill his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

Two causes for one event, laid side by side in a single sentence. A spoiled young man preferred flattery to counsel and split a nation. And it was a turn of affairs brought about by God, to keep a word he had spoken through a prophet.

This history has done exactly this before. When David counted the people, one account says Satan incited him and the other says the LORD did, and the king says twice over that the sin was his. The pattern is the same here. Nothing in verse 15 excuses Rehoboam, and the chapter has spent ten verses showing precisely how he earned it. Nothing in the ten verses puts the outcome beyond God's ordering either.

And notice which word God is keeping. Ahijah's prophecy was given because Solomon had gone after other gods — a chapter this book does not print. The Chronicler will not tell that story and will not pretend the division came out of nowhere. He names the prophet, names the word, and leaves the reason on the shelf where he left it in chapter 9.

verseByVerse.quote: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Each of you to your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So all Israel went to their tents. But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah. Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and the people of Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer from the crowd is not new. Somebody has said it before.

What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Each of you to your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David.

That is Sheba's revolt, word for word. A worthless man of Benjamin blew a trumpet in David's own lifetime and shouted almost exactly those lines, and every man of Israel went up after him, and it took Joab and a siege and a head thrown over a wall to end it. The words were remembered for two generations and were ready to be used again the moment a king gave them an occasion.

And the phrase they reach for to dismiss the dynasty is the son of Jesse. Saul used it when he could not say the name. Nabal used it to refuse a fugitive food. Here it is a whole nation's way of saying the family is nobody. And in a stronghold in the wilderness a man called Amasai had once been clothed with the Spirit and taken the same sneer and made it his oath — we are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse — and the chronicle of the kingdom uses it as David's own epitaph.

Then the king does the last thing anybody should have done. Told that the burden of forced labour is intolerable, King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor.

He sent the man in charge of the grievance to negotiate about the grievance. They stoned him to death in the road, and Rehoboam quickly mounted his chariot to flee to Jerusalem — a king running for his life from a coronation.

So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. The man who first wrote that was living while the northern kingdom still stood. By the time the Chronicler copied it, Israel had been gone for three hundred years, scattered by Assyria and never gathered. The rebellion outlasted the rebels, which is what rebellions do.

10.theology:
Verse 15 puts two causes behind one event without ranking them: the king did not listen, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by God to keep a word spoken through Ahijah. This history has done it before, over David's census, where one account names Satan and the other the LORD and the king says twice that the sin was his. Ten verses here show exactly how Rehoboam earned the outcome; one verse says it was ordered. Neither is withdrawn.

And the verb in verses 8 and 13 is the word this book keeps for forsaking God — the same one God used at the dedication when he wrote the epitaph for the ruined house. Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men. Forsaking has a smaller form, and it looks like a young man walking out of a room full of grey heads.
10.examples:
The old men's advice was one sentence and every verb in it gave ground: be good to them, please them, speak good words, and they will serve you forever. Men who had watched a kingdom run for forty years had concluded that authority is not held by asserting it.

The young men did not weigh the grievance or ask what the north might do. They told the king what he would enjoy saying, which is the whole service they rendered.

Told that the forced labour was intolerable, he sent the head of the forced labour. The crowd stoned him in the road, and the king drove home alone.

11.title: He Walked in the Way of David and Solomon
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.<sup>2</sup>But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God:<sup>3</sup>"Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin,<sup>4</sup>'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and returned and did not go against Jeroboam.<sup>5</sup>Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he built cities for defense in Judah.<sup>6</sup>He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,<sup>7</sup>Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam,<sup>8</sup>Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,<sup>9</sup>Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,<sup>10</sup>Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, fortified cities that are in Judah and in Benjamin.<sup>11</sup>He made the fortresses strong, and put commanders in them, and stores of food, oil, and wine.<sup>12</sup>And he put shields and spears in all the cities and made them very strong. So he held Judah and Benjamin.<sup>13</sup>And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places where they lived.<sup>14</sup>For the Levites left their common lands and their holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD,<sup>15</sup>and he appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made.<sup>16</sup>And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>17</sup>They strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.<sup>18</sup>Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse,<sup>19</sup>and she bore him sons, Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.<sup>20</sup>After her he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.<sup>21</sup>Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and concubines (he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters).<sup>22</sup>And Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king.<sup>23</sup>And he dealt wisely and distributed some of his sons through all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, in all the fortified cities, and he gave them abundant provisions and procured wives for them.
11.overview:
Rehoboam musters 180,000 men to retake the north and is stopped by the prophet Shemaiah — you shall not go up or fight against your relatives ... for this thing is from me — and the army goes home (vv. 1-4). He fortifies fifteen cities, Bethlehem first, and provisions them (vv. 5-12). Jeroboam expels the Levites and installs his own priests for the calves, so they abandon their lands and come south; and with them come people from every tribe who had set their hearts to seek the LORD (vv. 13-16). For three years they keep the kingdom secure (v. 17). The chapter ends on eighteen wives, sixty concubines, and the sons posted through the fortified cities (vv. 18-23).

The cities all face south and west, toward Egypt and Philistia. He had been told not to fight his brothers and had believed it enough to build his defences the other way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The War That Did Not Happen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam musters 180,000 chosen warriors from Judah and Benjamin to restore the kingdom (v. 1), and the word of the LORD comes to Shemaiah: You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me (vv. 2-4). They listen and go home. Rehoboam then fortifies fifteen cities — Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Adullam, Lachish, Hebron among them — puts commanders in them with stores of food, oil and wine, and distributes shields and spears (vv. 5-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The division was God's doing, and here he says so to the injured party. Rehoboam is not told that he was wronged and must forgive; he is told that the thing he wants to undo came from God, and to go home.
verseByVerse.examples: An army of a hundred and eighty thousand was raised and disbanded on one prophet's sentence. Whatever else is true of Rehoboam, the first thing recorded of him after Shechem is that he listened.

verseByVerse.quote: When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam. But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, 'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and returned and did not go against Jeroboam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gets home and raises an army. A hundred and eighty thousand picked men out of Judah and Benjamin, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.

It is the obvious response and, by the standards of the age, the responsible one. Ten tribes have walked out; a king who does nothing about it is finished. And then a prophet nobody has heard of stops the whole thing with three sentences.

Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives. Return every man to his home, for this thing is from me.

Two things in that. First, the enemy is renamed. Not Israel, not the rebels, not Jeroboam's faction — your relatives, your brothers. Whatever the constitutional position, the men on the other side of the line are family, and a prophet says so before a sword is drawn.

Second: for this thing is from me. God takes responsibility for the division to the face of the man who lost by it. The Chronicler had already said it from the outside a few verses earlier — a turn of affairs brought about by God — and now it is said to Rehoboam directly. He is not told that he was wronged and should be gracious about it. He is told that the catastrophe is God's, and to go home.

So they listened to the word of the LORD and returned and did not go against Jeroboam.

They listened. A hundred and eighty thousand men armed and mustered, a king with everything to lose and a legitimate claim, and one unknown prophet with a sentence — and the army goes home. It is the last thing anyone would have expected from the man in the previous chapter, and it is the first thing recorded of him afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and he built cities for defense in Judah. He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, fortified cities that are in Judah and in Benjamin. He made the fortresses strong, and put commanders in them, and stores of food, oil, and wine. And he put shields and spears in all the cities and made them very strong. So he held Judah and Benjamin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifteen cities are fortified, and the list opens with Bethlehem.

Then Etam and Tekoa, where a shepherd would one day be called to prophesy; Beth-zur, Soco, and Adullam, where David hid in a cave with four hundred men in debt and distress; Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, whose people twice betrayed David's hiding place to Saul; Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron.

He does the job thoroughly — commanders in each, stores of food and oil and wine, shields and spears distributed, and made them very strong. This is competent work, and the Chronicler records it without irony.

But look at the map. Almost every one of those towns lies south or west of Jerusalem, along the approaches from the Philistine plain and the road up from Egypt. He is not fortifying against the north at all. He has just been told not to fight his brothers, and he has believed it enough to build his defences facing the other way.

Which makes the next chapter worse. The wall he built was aimed at the right direction, and Egypt came through it anyway — because by then the problem was not the wall.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam throws the Levites out of their office and appoints his own priests for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made, so the priests and Levites leave their common lands and their holdings and come to Judah (vv. 13-15). With them come those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel ... from all the tribes of Israel (v. 16), and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon (v. 17). The chapter closes on the king's household: eighteen wives, sixty concubines, and his sons posted through the fortified cities (vv. 18-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 16 is a migration of ordinary worshippers. Not the clergy, who had lost their posts, but people from every tribe who had set their hearts to seek the LORD and were willing to leave a country to do it.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who walked south gave up land. Levites held common lands and holdings by law, and they abandoned them rather than serve at a golden calf.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places where they lived. For the Levites left their common lands and their holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD, and he appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made. And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers. They strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a movement of people, and it runs in one direction.
