16.text: <sup>1</sup>In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.<sup>2</sup>Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying,<sup>3</sup>"There is a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me."<sup>4</sup>And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, and they conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.<sup>5</sup>And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease.<sup>6</sup>Then King Asa took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them he built Geba and Mizpah.<sup>7</sup>At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, "Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you.<sup>8</sup>Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand.<sup>9</sup>For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars."<sup>10</sup>Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time.<sup>11</sup>The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.<sup>12</sup>In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians.<sup>13</sup>And Asa slept with his fathers, dying in the forty-first year of his reign.<sup>14</sup>They buried him in the tomb that he had cut for himself in the city of David. They laid him on a bier that had been filled with various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and they made a very great fire in his honor.
16.overview: Baasha blockades the road north, and Asa answers by taking silver and gold out of the temple treasury to hire Ben-hadad of Syria. It works: Syria raids Israel, Baasha withdraws, and Asa carries off the abandoned building stone (vv. 1-6). Hanani the seer then charges him with leaning on Syria rather than on God, and with losing more than he gained — the army of the king of Syria has escaped you — and tells him the eyes of the LORD range the whole earth looking for a whole heart (vv. 7-9). Asa jails the seer in the stocks and oppresses others (v. 10). Three years later a disease in his feet becomes severe and he does not seek the LORD; he dies in his forty-first year and is buried with great honour (vv. 11-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Silver Out of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the thirty-sixth year Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to blockade Judah (v. 1). Asa's answer is a transaction: he took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad of Syria, asking him to break his treaty with Baasha (vv. 2-3). Ben-hadad listens, raids the northern towns, and Baasha stops building (vv. 4-5). Asa then carries off the stones and timber of Ramah and builds Geba and Mizpah with them (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: It worked. Baasha withdrew, the blockade lifted, and Asa even got the building materials. Everything about the policy succeeded, which is precisely what the prophet is about to object to.
verseByVerse.examples: The payment came out of the house of the LORD. Twenty years earlier this king had brought his father's sacred gifts and his own into that treasury; now he is taking money out of it to hire a foreign army.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying, "There is a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me." And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, and they conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali. And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease. Then King Asa took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them he built Geba and Mizpah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baasha of Israel comes down and fortifies Ramah, five miles north of Jerusalem, specifically that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. It is a blockade on the main road, and it is aimed at the migration — the people who had been coming south because they saw that the LORD was with Asa.

The date is given as the thirty-sixth year, which does not fit the other account, where Baasha is dead by Asa's twenty-sixth. The usual suggestions are a reckoning from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa's accession, or a numeral copied wrongly. Nothing in the chapter turns on it.

What Asa does is efficient. Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad king of Syria.

Notice where the money came from. One chapter ago he brought his father's sacred gifts and his own into that treasury. Now he is taking silver out of it, and the temple funds a foreign general.

The message is a piece of ordinary statecraft: there is a treaty between us as there was between our fathers, here is silver, break your treaty with Baasha. He is buying a man who has already shown he will sell.

And it works perfectly. Ben-hadad raids Ijon and Dan and Abel-maim and the store cities of Naphtali; Baasha abandons Ramah; and Asa turns up with all Judah and carries off the stones and timber his enemy had stockpiled, and builds Geba and Mizpah with them. He has lifted the blockade, humiliated his rival and acquired free building materials, in one move.

There is nothing incompetent here at all. That is the difficulty the next three verses address.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — The Eyes of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hanani the seer arrives with one word repeated: because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you (v. 7). The Ethiopians had been a far bigger force, yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand (v. 8). Then the reason it matters: for the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him — and the sentence, from now on you will have wars (v. 9). Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, and inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is not that the alliance failed. It is that it worked, and cost him more than it bought: Syria walked away intact, when leaning on God would have delivered both armies. A solution that succeeds can still be the expensive option.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 has God scanning the earth for somebody to back. The eyes that Solomon asked to be open toward one building are described here as running to and fro over the whole of it, looking for a heart that is whole.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, "Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you. Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand. For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah.

And the word he brings turns on one verb, used three times in two verses. It means to lean your weight onto a thing.

Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you.

That verb has a history in this family. Asa's father stood surrounded on a hillside in Ephraim and Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD. Asa himself, outnumbered nearly two to one by an Ethiopian army, prayed we rely on you, and the LORD defeated them. He knows the word. He has used it correctly under far worse pressure.

And then read what Hanani actually charges him with, because it is not what anyone expects. The army of the king of Syria has escaped you.

The complaint is not that the policy failed. It is that it succeeded and cost him something larger. Syria was in the field; had Asa leaned on God as he had done at Mareshah, Ben-hadad's army would have been given into his hand along with Baasha's. Instead he paid silver to a man who is now stronger, richer and still at large, and who will be back in his grandson's reign, and his great-grandson's.

Verse 8 makes the comparison explicit. The Ethiopians were a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen — far worse odds than Baasha ever presented — and God handed them over. The bigger crisis was met by leaning on God; the smaller one was met by opening the treasury. Small troubles are more dangerous than large ones for exactly this reason: they look manageable.

Then verse 9, and it lifts out of the chapter.

For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him.

God is not waiting to be asked. He is described as scanning — the eyes going back and forth over the whole earth, actively looking for somebody to put his strength behind. Solomon had asked, at the dedication, that God's eyes would be open toward one building, and God had answered that his eyes and his heart would be there. Here the same eyes are ranging over the entire world.

And what they are looking for is not competence or success or even faithfulness in general. A heart that is whole toward him — undivided, all pointing one way. Asa had one at Mareshah. He did not have one at Ramah, and the eyes that had been ranging the earth found him leaning on Damascus.

The sentence is short: you have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars. The rest that had defined the reign is over, and the reason is a single decision that worked.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks in prison, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time.

This is the man who cut down his grandmother's idol and burned it at the Kidron, who repaired a neglected altar, who took courage the instant a prophet spoke to him and cleared the idols out of three territories.

The last time a prophet came to Asa, in chapter 15, the response was immediate obedience. This time the prophet goes in the stocks — a public restraint, designed to humiliate as much as to hold — and the king is described as being in a rage.

And the last clause is the one that shows how far it has gone. And Asa inflicted cruelties upon some of the people at the same time. Not only the seer. Others, unnamed, in the same period, because a man who cannot bear one voice telling him the truth usually cannot bear several.

Thirty-five years of rest, reform and answered prayer, and it turns out that what he could not survive was being corrected while he was right about the outcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The acts of Asa are on record (v. 11). In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians (v. 12). He dies in his forty-first year (v. 13) and is buried in the tomb he had cut for himself, on a bier filled with spices prepared by the perfumer's art, with a very great fire in his honor (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 12 is the one Asa himself put on the whole nation at the start of his reign, when he commanded Judah to seek the LORD. Forty years later he is the man of whom it is said that he did not.
verseByVerse.examples: They buried him with every honour Judah could pay — his own cut tomb, spices by the perfumer's art, a great fire. The nation did not think less of him at the end than it had at the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: The acts of Asa, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians. And Asa slept with his fathers, dying in the forty-first year of his reign. They buried him in the tomb that he had cut for himself in the city of David. They laid him on a bier that had been filled with various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and they made a very great fire in his honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians.

The verb is the one that has followed him through four chapters. He commanded Judah to seek the LORD in his first year; a prophet told him that if he sought him he would be found; a whole nation swore a covenant to seek him with their whole desire and he was found by them. Now, in pain, at the end, the chronicle says he did not seek him.

One thing has to be said plainly, because this verse has been used to wound sick people. It is not a criticism of doctors. Scripture nowhere treats medicine as a rival to faith — Isaiah prescribed a fig poultice for a dying king, Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach, and Luke, who wrote a quarter of the New Testament, was a physician and is called the beloved one. There is nothing in this book against a man consulting the best help he can find.

The charge is in the first half of the clause. He did not seek the LORD — and then, having not sought him, he went looking elsewhere. It is the omission that is named, not the consultation. Had he sought God and called the physicians, no one would have written this sentence. He sought help everywhere except the one place he had spent his reign telling the country to look.

And that is the shape of the whole decline. Not a conversion to idolatry — there is no Asherah at the end of Asa's life. Just a slow narrowing, from a man who prayed four sentences against a million men, to a man who bought an alliance, to a man who jailed the person who told him about it, to a man in agony who would ask anybody but God.

He is buried with everything Judah could give him: a tomb he had cut for himself, a bier heaped with spices prepared by the perfumer's art, and a very great fire in his honor. The nation thought well of him at the end, and the nation was not wrong to. The Chronicler has already given his verdict — that the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days — and he does not withdraw it, and he does not tidy away the last five years either.

Both stand. A life can be genuinely turned toward God and end badly, and the God whose eyes run to and fro throughout the whole earth looking for a whole heart is the one who keeps both records.

16.theology:
One verb carries the whole Asa cycle: sha'an, to lean your weight onto a thing. Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD (13:18); Asa prayed we rely on you against a million men (14:11); and Hanani uses it three times in two verses to say he leaned on Damascus instead. The indictment is not that the alliance failed — it succeeded completely. It is that Syria escaped, when leaning on God would have delivered both armies. A small crisis is more dangerous than a large one because it looks manageable.

Verse 9 shows God scanning rather than waiting: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him. Solomon had asked that those eyes be open toward one building; here they range over the world, looking for an undivided heart to back.
16.examples:
⚠️ Verse 12 is not a verdict on medicine. Isaiah prescribed a poultice for a dying king, Paul told Timothy to take wine for his stomach, and Luke the physician wrote a quarter of the New Testament. The charge is the omission in the first half of the clause — he did not seek the LORD — and then went looking everywhere else. Had he sought God and called the doctors, nobody would have written the sentence.

What ruined him was a decision that worked. Nothing about the Syrian alliance was incompetent; it lifted a blockade and produced free building materials. He could not bear being corrected while he was right about the outcome, and the prophet went into the stocks.

The decline was not a conversion to idolatry. There is no Asherah at the end of Asa's life — only a slow narrowing, from a man who prayed four sentences against a million to a man in agony who would ask anybody but God.

17.title: He Sought the God of His Father
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place and strengthened himself against Israel.<sup>2</sup>He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah and set garrisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had captured.<sup>3</sup>The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals,<sup>4</sup>but sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments, and not according to the practices of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand. And all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had great riches and honor.<sup>6</sup>His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD. And furthermore, he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah.<sup>7</sup>In the third year of his reign he sent his officials, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah;<sup>8</sup>and with them the Levites, Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah; and with these Levites, the priests Elishama and Jehoram.<sup>9</sup>And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.<sup>10</sup>And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat.<sup>11</sup>Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute, and the Arabians also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.<sup>12</sup>And Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. He built in Judah fortresses and store cities,<sup>13</sup>and he had large supplies in the cities of Judah. He had soldiers, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>This was the muster of them by fathers' houses: Of Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty men of valor;<sup>15</sup>and next to him Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000;<sup>16</sup>and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men of valor.<sup>17</sup>Of Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with 200,000 men armed with bow and shield;<sup>18</sup>and next to him Jehozabad with 180,000 armed for war.<sup>19</sup>These were in the service of the king, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.
17.overview: Jehoshaphat secures the country and is commended before the reign has done anything: he did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father, and his heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD (vv. 1-6). In his third year he sends five officials, nine Levites and two priests on circuit through every city of Judah having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them (vv. 7-9). The fear of the LORD falls on the surrounding kingdoms and nobody attacks him; tribute comes in and he builds (vv. 10-13). The chapter closes with a muster of more than a million men, one of whom is described rather than counted: a volunteer for the service of the LORD (vv. 14-19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Book Taken Round the Cities
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoshaphat garrisons the country (vv. 1-2), and the LORD is with him because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father (vv. 3-4). The kingdom is established, tribute comes in (v. 5), and his heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD — the high places and the Asherim come out (v. 6). Then, in his third year, he sends five named officials, nine Levites and two priests out to teach, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Two chapters ago a prophet diagnosed Israel's long collapse as a nation without a teaching priest and without law. Jehoshaphat repairs precisely that, and sends royal officials along with the Levites so that nobody could treat it as an optional religious programme.
verseByVerse.examples: The heart described in verse 6 is literally a HIGH heart, and the same phrase condemns two later kings of Judah for pride. What makes it a virtue here is the phrase attached to it: high in the ways of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place and strengthened himself against Israel. He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah and set garrisons in the land of Judah, and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had captured. The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments, and not according to the practices of Israel. Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand. And all Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had great riches and honor. His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD. And furthermore, he took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign opens with security measures — garrisons in the fortified cities and in the towns his father had taken in Ephraim — and then the Chronicler gives his verdict before the reign has done anything.

The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David.

The qualifier is doing work. Not the ways of David, but the earlier ways — David before the roof and the letter and the census, the man in the cave and the barley field and the tent with the ark in it. The model held up to a new king is another man's best period rather than his whole record. Some read the Hebrew as pointing to his own father's early years instead, which would be sharper still after chapter 16, where Asa ended in the stocks and the sickroom.

Then the same verb twice, once each way: He did not seek the Baals, but sought the God of his father. Seeking is not optional; everyone does it. The question the Chronicler always asks is what a man is seeking, and the sentence is built to force the comparison.

And verse 6 gives a description of his heart that would be an accusation anywhere else in this book. His heart was courageous in the ways of the LORD.

The Hebrew says his heart was high — lifted up. When Uzziah's heart is lifted up he goes into the temple with a censer and comes out a leper. When Hezekiah's heart is lifted up wrath comes on Judah. The identical phrase, twice condemned.

What makes it a virtue here is the four words attached to it: high in the ways of the LORD. A raised heart is not the problem; what it is raised about is. Take the same confidence and point it at yourself and it is pride; point it at God's commandments and it is the nerve to take down the high places your father left standing.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of his reign he sent his officials, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah; and with them the Levites, Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah; and with these Levites, the priests Elishama and Jehoram. And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his third year he does something no other king in Scripture does.

He sent his officials, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah; and with them the Levites ... and with these Levites, the priests Elishama and Jehoram. And they taught in Judah, having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.

Sixteen men, named individually, sent out on circuit with a book.

Two chapters ago the prophet Azariah stood in front of Jehoshaphat's father and diagnosed four centuries of Israel's history in one line: they were without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law. Not without priests. Without any who taught. The office survived and the instruction stopped, and the nation went dark.

Jehoshaphat repairs exactly that. And the composition of the party is deliberate: royal officials at the head of it, then the Levites, then two priests. The crown is standing behind the teaching, so that no town could treat the visit as an optional religious event put on by the clergy.

They went about through all the cities. Not a festival in Jerusalem that people might come up to — a circuit of every town, with the book, on the road, for as long as it took. It is the least glamorous reform in the book of Chronicles, and the next verse reports what came of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — The Fear of the LORD, and the Muster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat (v. 10). Philistines bring tribute and Arabians bring 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats (v. 11). He builds fortresses and store cities and keeps large supplies (vv. 12-13). The muster follows by fathers' houses — Adnah with 300,000, Jehohanan with 280,000, Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD, with 200,000, and two Benjaminite commanders with 380,000 between them — besides the garrisons (vv. 14-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching mission is what stands between verse 9 and verse 10. Nobody made war on him, and the Chronicler places that fact immediately after the Book of the Law going round the towns.
verseByVerse.examples: In a list that is nothing but names and totals, one man gets a description: he volunteered. Somebody thought it worth recording that Amasiah was not conscripted.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat. Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute, and the Arabians also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats. And Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. He built in Judah fortresses and store cities, and he had large supplies in the cities of Judah. He had soldiers, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat.

The Chronicler puts that sentence immediately after the teaching mission, and the sequence is his argument. A king sends the law round his own villages and the surrounding nations stop attacking him. Nothing in between is described — no campaign, no treaty, no show of force.

Philistines who had been raiding the lowlands for centuries send tribute. Arabians bring seven thousand seven hundred rams and the same number of goats, which is a herdsman's way of saying a great deal.

And Jehoshaphat grew steadily greater. Fortresses, store cities, large supplies, and soldiers in Jerusalem. The growth is reported as a consequence rather than an achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the muster of them by fathers' houses: Of Judah, the commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty men of valor; and next to him Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000; and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men of valor. Of Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with 200,000 men armed with bow and shield; and next to him Jehozabad with 180,000 armed for war. These were in the service of the king, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The muster is by fathers' houses and it is enormous: three hundred thousand under Adnah, two hundred and eighty thousand under Jehohanan, two hundred thousand under Amasiah, and from Benjamin two hundred thousand archers under Eliada and a hundred and eighty thousand under Jehozabad. More than a million men, besides those whom the king had placed in the fortified cities.

The Hebrew word behind a thousand can also mean a unit or a contingent, which may account for figures on this scale here and elsewhere in these books. What the register is plainly recording is a country that had become, in twenty years, too strong to be worth attacking.

And in the middle of the totals one man is described rather than counted.

Amasiah the son of Zichri, a volunteer for the service of the LORD.

Everyone else in the list is a commander with a number. This one has a phrase attached: he offered himself. In a kingdom with conscription, garrisons and a standing levy, somebody kept a note that Amasiah was not called up — and it went into the permanent record of the reign, and it is the only thing anybody knows about him.

17.theology:
The teaching mission repairs precisely what Azariah had diagnosed two chapters earlier — Israel without a teaching priest and without law. The office had survived and the instruction had stopped. Jehoshaphat sends the Book of the Law round every town with royal officials at the head of the party, so that no village could treat it as an optional religious event, and the Chronicler puts the surrounding nations' fear of the LORD in the very next verse.

Verse 6 then describes a HIGH heart and commends it, where the identical phrase condemns Uzziah and Hezekiah for pride. The difference is the four words attached: high in the ways of the LORD. Confidence pointed at yourself is arrogance; pointed at God's commandments it is the nerve to pull down what your father left standing.
17.examples:
The reform was a circuit of every town with a book, on the road, for as long as it took — the least glamorous thing any king in this book does, and the Chronicler makes it the reason nobody made war on him.

The model held up to him was the earlier ways of David: another man's best period rather than his whole record.

In a register of a million conscripts, one man is described instead of counted — Amasiah, a volunteer for the service of the LORD. It is the only thing anybody knows about him, and somebody thought it worth writing down.

18.title: Is There Not Here Another Prophet of the LORD?
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab.<sup>2</sup>After some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. And Ahab killed an abundance of sheep and oxen for him and for the people who were with him, and induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.<sup>3</sup>Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" He answered him, "I am as you are, my people as your people. We will be with you in the war."<sup>4</sup>And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD."<sup>5</sup>Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall we go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>6</sup>But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?"<sup>7</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."<sup>8</sup>Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah."<sup>9</sup>Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. And they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.<sup>10</sup>And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"<sup>11</sup>And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>12</sup>And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably."<sup>13</sup>But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak."<sup>14</sup>And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?" And he answered, "Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand."<sup>15</sup>But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"<sup>16</sup>And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'"<sup>17</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"<sup>18</sup>And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab the king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another.<sup>20</sup>Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?'<sup>21</sup>And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.'<sup>22</sup>Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. The LORD has declared disaster concerning you."<sup>23</sup>Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"<sup>24</sup>And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."<sup>25</sup>And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,<sup>26</sup>and say, 'Thus says the king, Put this fellow in prison and feed him with meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace.'"<sup>27</sup>And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"<sup>28</sup>So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>29</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.<sup>30</sup>Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel."<sup>31</sup>As soon as the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him.<sup>32</sup>For as soon as the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.<sup>33</sup>But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded."<sup>34</sup>And the battle continued that day, and the king of Israel was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. Then at sunset he died.
18.overview: Jehoshaphat's wealth makes him worth marrying into, and he allies his house with Ahab's (v. 1). Feasted in Samaria and pressed to join a campaign, he commits his army first and asks for a word from the LORD second (vv. 2-4). Four hundred prophets say go; he asks for another, and Ahab names Micaiah, whom he hates for always being right (vv. 5-11). Micaiah refuses to be coached, mocks the king with the expected answer, and then gives the true one — Israel scattered as sheep without a shepherd — followed by the vision of the heavenly council and the lying spirit (vv. 12-22). He is struck, jailed on bread and water, and stakes his standing on the outcome (vv. 23-27). Ahab disguises himself and dresses Jehoshaphat as bait; God rescues Jehoshaphat, and an arrow shot at random kills Ahab (vv. 28-34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — A Marriage, and Four Hundred Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab (v. 1). Years later Ahab feasts him in Samaria and induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead (v. 2). Asked to come, Jehoshaphat commits first — I am as you are, my people as your people — and only then says inquire first for the word of the LORD (vv. 3-4). Four hundred prophets say go (v. 5), but Jehoshaphat asks whether there is another, and Ahab names Micaiah: I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me (vv. 6-8). The two kings sit in their robes at the threshing floor by the gate while Zedekiah makes iron horns and the whole company prophesies victory (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 1 puts the wealth and the marriage in a single sentence, and this book alone does that. Chapter 17 had already reported the riches and honour as God's gift; here they are the reason the house of Omri wanted him as a relative, and the bride's family will nearly destroy the house of David.
verseByVerse.examples: He said inquire first after he had already promised his army. The word first is doing no work by the time he uses it, and everything that follows in this chapter is a man looking for permission he has already given away.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab. After some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. And Ahab killed an abundance of sheep and oxen for him and for the people who were with him, and induced him to go up against Ramoth-gilead. Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" He answered him, "I am as you are, my people as your people. We will be with you in the war."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab.

Two facts in one sentence, and only this book puts them there. The riches and honour were reported a chapter ago as the consequence of a king who sought God rather than the Baals. Here they are the thing that made him worth marrying into.

Prosperity has a social effect that poverty does not. A strong, wealthy, well-governed Judah is a country the house of Omri wants a treaty with, and treaties in that world were sealed in the bedroom. What God gave him made him attractive to the worst family in Israel.

The marriage is not described here, and it should be named because everything terrible in the next five chapters comes out of it. Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram married Athaliah, Ahab's daughter. She will watch her son die and then kill every royal child she can find, and the line of David will survive by one infant hidden in a bedroom for six years. That is what verse 1 is the seed of, and the verse says nothing at all about it.

Then the visit. Ahab kills sheep and oxen in abundance for him and induced him — the word means enticed, talked round — to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

And Jehoshaphat's answer is total before a single question has been asked. I am as you are, my people as your people. We will be with you in the war.

He has committed his army, his nation and himself, to a campaign he knows nothing about, for a king whose wife is murdering prophets. He is a good man, and this is what a good man sounds like when he has been made much of by somebody powerful.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD." Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall we go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king." But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, Inquire first for the word of the LORD.

First. He says the word after promising everything. The instinct is right and it has arrived one sentence too late, and the whole chapter turns on that gap. Everything he does from here is the behaviour of a man looking for permission he has already given away.

And note the verb he uses, because it is this book's own and it comes three times in four verses. Inquire for the word of the LORD; is there not another prophet of whom we may inquire; there is yet one man by whom we may inquire. The word behind it is the one the Chronicler has been using since Saul's obituary — to seek. Two kings are about to spend a whole afternoon seeking, and only one of them wants an answer he has not already chosen.

Four hundred prophets are assembled and asked a closed question, and they give the answer the question was shaped for: Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king. They are not described as prophets of Baal. They use God's name and they are unanimous.

And Jehoshaphat is not satisfied. Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?

Four hundred men have just agreed with each other, and something in the sound of it is wrong to him. It is the best moment of his day. He cannot say what is missing and he knows that unanimity is not the same as a word from God.

Ahab's reply is one of the most self-revealing sentences any king ever spoke. There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil.

He does not say Micaiah is a liar. He says the man is always right about him and he hates him for it. Ahab has kept a genuine prophet on the register, available, in Samaria, for years — and has organised his life so as never to have to listen to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah." Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. And they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them. And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'" And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The LORD will give it into the hand of the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is set with some care. Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes. And they were sitting at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.

Two thrones, full royal dress, the open space by the city gate where business was done, and four hundred men performing. It is a stage, and the verdict has been reached before the witness arrives.

Zedekiah has made himself iron horns and works the crowd with them: Thus says the LORD, With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed. He has read his Bible — the horns are Moses' blessing on Joseph — and he has props, and he speaks in the formula. Everything about him is correct except that God has not spoken to him.

And verse 11 gives their line in full, because it is about to be used again: Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. The LORD will give it into the hand of the king. They had said it in verse 5 and they say it again here, with one accord, in the same words.

The verdict has been reached. All that is missing is the witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — What My God Says, That I Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messenger coaches Micaiah to agree with the others, and gets an oath in reply: As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak (vv. 12-13). He then says go up and triumph in a tone Ahab can hear, and is put on oath (vv. 14-15). The real word follows: I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd (vv. 16-17). And then the vision behind it — the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven, asking who will entice Ahab; a spirit volunteering to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets; and the answer, you shall succeed; go out and do so (vv. 18-21). Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Whatever else is true of verses 18-22, notice what Micaiah does with the vision: he tells the man it is about, to his face, before the army moves. A deception announced in advance to its intended victim has stopped functioning as a deception and become a final warning.
verseByVerse.examples: The messenger's advice is the oldest pressure there is — the others all agree, so make your word like one of theirs. Micaiah answers it with an oath rather than an argument.

verseByVerse.quote: And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably." But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak." And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?" And he answered, "Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand." But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?" And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officer sent to fetch Micaiah gives him some advice on the road. Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably.

It is the oldest pressure in the world and it is offered kindly. Everyone agrees; the king wants to hear it; be like one of them. Not lie, exactly — just match. The messenger is probably trying to save the man's life.

But Micaiah said, As the LORD lives, what my God says, that I will speak.

He answers an argument with an oath, which is the only way to answer that particular argument, because there is no counter-case to make against four hundred men. And the possessive should be noticed: the account in Kings has what the LORD says, and this book has what my God says. Micaiah is not citing an office or a rule. He is naming a person he belongs to.

Then he arrives and says exactly what he was told to say — and he says it in their words. Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand.

Those are the four hundred's own words, twice on record in this chapter, handed back over the counter. Micaiah has not invented a line; he has repeated theirs, which is why the tone is unmistakable. A man who agrees with you in your own words, exactly, is not agreeing with you.

And Ahab, who has never listened to this man in his life, hears the tone instantly. How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD? The irony is total: the king is now demanding the truth from the one man who always tells it, in a room full of people he has assembled to avoid it.

So Micaiah gives it. I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.

The picture is not of an army defeated but of a flock with nobody in front of it. Moses had used the same phrase when he asked God for a successor so that the congregation would not be as sheep without a shepherd. Centuries later a man looked out over a crowd in Galilee and had compassion on them for precisely that reason, and began to teach them.

What Micaiah is telling Ahab is that the campaign will end with the king dead and the army wandering home. And Ahab turns to his guest and says, in effect, I told you so — did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil? He has heard the content and filed it as a character trait.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left. And the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab the king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. The LORD has declared disaster concerning you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Micaiah opens the curtain, and what he shows is the hardest thing here to hold.

I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left. And the LORD said, Who will entice Ahab the king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? ... Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, I will entice him ... I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.

And then the application, delivered to Ahab's face: the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets. The LORD has declared disaster concerning you.

Take the difficulty head on, because it is real. Scripture says elsewhere and without qualification that God is not a man that he should lie, and that he cannot lie. This vision shows him presiding over a council in which a deceiving spirit is commissioned and sent. Both are in the Bible and neither is going to be withdrawn.

Three things can be said, and the third is the one that matters most.

First, God does not speak the lie. He permits and directs a spirit that is already willing, and every word of falsehood is spoken by Zedekiah and his four hundred out of their own mouths, for their own reasons — a court prophet's living depends on telling a king what he wants. Nobody in that gateway was forced to say anything.

Second, this is judgement, not entrapment. Ahab has spent a reign refusing the truth. He has killed prophets, married Jezebel, hunted Elijah, and by his own account keeps Micaiah at arm's length because the man is always right. There comes a point in the New Testament where the same principle is stated flatly: because they refused to love the truth and so be saved, God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false. The delusion is not the beginning of the story. It is the settlement of an account.

And third — this is the point that dissolves most of the difficulty, and it is right here in the text. Micaiah tells him.

The deception is announced to its intended victim, in public, before a horse has moved. Ahab is standing in his robes on a throne and is told, in plain words, that the four hundred men who have just promised him victory are speaking under a lying spirit and that God has declared disaster concerning him. He has the truth. He has it from a prophet whose accuracy he has himself certified, in front of a witness.

A deception you have been warned about, by name, in advance, has stopped being a deception. It has become a last offer. And what Ahab does with it is arrest the man who brought it and go to war in disguise — which is the behaviour of somebody who believed every word and intended to outmanoeuvre it anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — A Bow Drawn at Random
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zedekiah strikes Micaiah on the cheek and asks which way the Spirit went to reach him (v. 23); Micaiah tells him he will find out on the day he hides in an inner room (v. 24). Ahab jails him on bread and water until I return in peace, and gets the answer: if you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me (vv. 25-27). They go up. Ahab disguises himself and tells Jehoshaphat to wear his robes (vv. 28-29); the Syrians have orders to fight only the king of Israel and go for the man in the robes — and Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him (vv. 30-32). Then a certain man drew his bow at random and hit Ahab through a joint in the armour, and he died at sunset (vv. 33-34).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 31 is this book's own. The other account has Jehoshaphat cry out and the chariots turn away; only Chronicles says the LORD helped him and God drew them off. The king who should not have been there was rescued anyway.
verseByVerse.examples: The disguise worked and it made no difference. An archer who was aiming at nobody in particular put an arrow through the one gap in the armour of the one man the whole battle was about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?" And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself." And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son, and say, 'Thus says the king, Put this fellow in prison and feed him with meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace.'" And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah's response is a slap. Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?

It is a genuine question in a sarcastic voice, and it assumes the thing under dispute — that the Spirit was in him to begin with. Micaiah's answer is not an argument either. Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself. You will know which of us was speaking for God on the day you are looking for somewhere to hide.

Then the king disposes of him: prison, and meager rations of bread and water until I return in peace. It is not an execution. Ahab is confident enough to plan a conversation afterwards.

And Micaiah gets the last word, and stakes his own standing on it. If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me.

That is the test the law itself lays down for a prophet, and he applies it to himself in front of the court. If the king walks back through this gate, I am a false prophet and you may treat me as one. Then, turning from the king to everyone standing there: Hear, all you peoples!

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle. Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel." As soon as the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him. For as soon as the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded." And the battle continued that day, and the king of Israel was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening. Then at sunset he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. Both of them. The man who asked for another prophet, and got one, and heard him, goes anyway.

Then Ahab makes his arrangement. I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes.

Read that slowly. He believes Micaiah — the disguise is only intelligible if he does — and his solution is to make his ally the most conspicuous man on the field while he himself goes in as an anonymous soldier. He is not asking Jehoshaphat to take a risk. He is using him as a decoy, and Jehoshaphat agrees to it.

The Syrians have orders to fight nobody but the king of Israel, so the chariot captains see a man in royal robes and turn on him. And then this book says something the other account does not.

And Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him.

In Kings, Jehoshaphat cries out and the captains realise their mistake and turn back. Chronicles keeps that and puts two clauses in front of it: the LORD helped him, God drew them away. The king who should never have been in that battle, dressed as bait by a man who was deceiving him, shouts in the middle of a chariot charge and God gets him out.

Sit with that, because it is not a reward. Jehoshaphat had promised his army before asking, asked afterwards, heard the true word, and marched. He was wrong at every stage and God rescued him at the last one — and a prophet will be waiting for him at the door when he gets home.

Then the arrow. But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate.

At random. Nobody aimed at Ahab; nobody could, because nobody could see him. An unnamed soldier let one go in the general direction of the enemy, and it found the single unarmoured seam in the one man the entire day was about.

He had taken the only precaution available to him and it was a good one, and it was beaten by chance — which in this book is another word for something else. He is propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians all afternoon so the army will not break, and at sunset he dies, and the men go home to their tents like sheep that have no shepherd.

18.theology:
The vision of verses 18-22 has to be held with both hands. Scripture says plainly that God cannot lie, and here he presides over a council in which a deceiving spirit is commissioned. Three things stand. God speaks no lie: the falsehood comes out of Zedekiah's own mouth for his own reasons. It is judgement rather than entrapment, on a man who had spent a reign refusing the truth — the principle the New Testament states flatly when it says that because they refused to love the truth, God sends them a strong delusion.

And the third point dissolves most of the difficulty: Micaiah tells him. The deception is announced to its intended victim, in public, before the army moves. A deception you have been warned about by name in advance has stopped being a deception and become a last offer — and Ahab's response, to jail the messenger and go to war in disguise, is the behaviour of a man who believed every word and meant to outmanoeuvre it.

Against that stands verse 31, which only this book has. Jehoshaphat was wrong at every stage — promising first, asking second, hearing the truth and marching anyway — and when the chariots turned on him, the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him. It is not a reward. There is a prophet waiting at his door in the next chapter.
18.examples:
He said inquire first after he had already promised his army, his people and himself. The instinct was right and it arrived one sentence too late, and everything afterwards is a man looking for permission he had already given away.

The whole company agreed, and something in the sound of it was wrong to him. He could not say what was missing and he knew unanimity is not the same as a word from God. It is the best moment of his day.

The messenger's advice was kind and is the oldest pressure there is: they all agree, so make your word like one of theirs. Not lie — just match. Micaiah answered it with an oath, because there is no argument to be made against four hundred people.

19.title: Fear the LORD and Act Faithfully
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned in safety to his house in Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God."<sup>4</sup>Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>5</sup>He appointed judges in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city,<sup>6</sup>and said to the judges, "Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment.<sup>7</sup>Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes."<sup>8</sup>Moreover, in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed certain Levites and priests and heads of families of Israel, to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases. They had their seat at Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>And he charged them: "Thus you shall do in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart:<sup>10</sup>whenever a case comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities, concerning bloodshed, law or commandment, statutes or rules, then you shall warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. Thus you shall do, and you will not incur guilt.<sup>11</sup>And behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the governor of the house of Judah, in all the king's matters, and the Levites will serve you as officers. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright!"
19.overview: Jehoshaphat gets home alive and Jehu the son of Hanani meets him with a rebuke — should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? — and, in the same breath, a commendation: nevertheless, some good is found in you ... you have set your heart to seek God (vv. 1-3). He responds by going out himself, the length of the country, bringing the people back (v. 4). Then he appoints judges in every fortified city and tells them they judge not for man but for the LORD, on a standard that is God's own character (vv. 5-7); and he seats an appeal court at Jerusalem with two heads, one for the LORD's matters and one for the king's (vv. 8-11).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoshaphat gets home alive (v. 1), and Jehu the son of Hanani meets him at the door: Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD (v. 2). Then the other half: Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The seer who says this is the son of the seer Asa jailed. Hanani told Asa he had leaned on the wrong king and went into the stocks for it; his son says something harder to Asa's son and walks away. The office ran in that family, and so did the risk.
verseByVerse.examples: The rebuke has a nevertheless in it. God's assessment of a man who has just come back from the worst decision of his reign includes what is good in him, named specifically, and neither half cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned in safety to his house in Jerusalem. But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned in safety to his house in Jerusalem.

In safety, which is the point of the previous chapter's thirty-first verse: he was dressed as bait, the chariots came for him, he shouted, and God drew them off. He is alive because of a rescue he did nothing to earn.

And a man is waiting for him. But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him.

Hanani is a name from three chapters ago. He is the seer who told Asa that he had leaned on the king of Syria instead of on the LORD, and Asa put him in the stocks in a rage and oppressed some of the people at the same time. That was this man's father.

So the son walks out to meet Asa's son at the gate of Jerusalem, knowing exactly what the job costs in this family, and says: Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the LORD.

Two verbs, and the second is the sharper. Help the wicked is what the alliance did. Love those who hate the LORD is what it revealed. Jehoshaphat did not merely make a calculation about Ramoth-gilead; he liked Ahab, he had married into the family, and he had said I am as you are, my people as your people to a man whose wife was killing prophets.

And then the word turns, and this is what makes the chapter worth having.

Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God.

God's assessment of a man on the worst day of his reign includes what is good in him, itemised. He pulled down the Asherah poles. He set his heart to seek God — which is the exact phrase used of the people who left the north to come south under Rehoboam, and the exact thing the chronicle said Rehoboam himself never did.

Wrath has gone out, and some good is found. Both are true of the same man in the same breath, and neither is a qualification of the other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — You Judge Not for Man but for the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He goes out again among the people himself, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brings them back to the LORD (v. 4). He appoints judges city by city through the fortified towns (v. 5) and charges them: Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment (v. 6); let the fear of the LORD be upon you ... for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes (v. 7). At Jerusalem he seats a second court of Levites, priests and heads of families to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases (v. 8), charged to act in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart (v. 9), and to warn litigants so that guilt falls on nobody (v. 10). Two heads are named — Amariah for the LORD's matters, Zebadiah for the king's — and the charge ends: Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright! (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: A judge is told that his bench is not his own. He judges for the LORD, God stands with him while he does it, and the standard is God's own character — no injustice, no partiality, no bribes. The three things forbidden are the three ways a court actually goes wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 puts the judge's own neck in the case. He is to warn the parties so that they do not incur guilt and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. A bad verdict does not stay with the litigants.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. He appointed judges in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city, and said to the judges, "Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment. Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What he does with the rebuke is the measure of him. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.

Again — because he had done it in his third year, when he sent five officials and nine Levites and two priests round the towns with the Book of the Law. This time he goes himself, the length of the country, from the southern desert to the northern hills.

Then the judiciary, and it is the most detailed constitutional arrangement in these two books. Judges appointed in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city — not a central tribunal people must travel to, but a bench in every walled town.

And the charge he gives them is theological before it is procedural.

Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD. He is with you in giving judgment.

The bench is not the judge's own. He is not administering the king's law on the king's behalf; he is doing God's work, in God's place, and God is standing with him while he does it. That is a terrifying thing to be told before a day's hearings and a great comfort in the middle of one.

Then the standard, and it is not a code but a character. Now then, let the fear of the LORD be upon you. Be careful what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes.

Three things are named because they are the three ways a court actually fails: a wrong verdict, a verdict bent toward the important party, and a verdict bought. Judges are not told to be fair in the abstract. They are told what God is like and instructed to match.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed certain Levites and priests and heads of families of Israel, to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases. They had their seat at Jerusalem. And he charged them: "Thus you shall do in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart: whenever a case comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities, concerning bloodshed, law or commandment, statutes or rules, then you shall warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. Thus you shall do, and you will not incur guilt. And behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the governor of the house of Judah, in all the king's matters, and the Levites will serve you as officers. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second court is seated in Jerusalem — Levites, priests and heads of families — to give judgment for the LORD and to decide disputed cases. It is an appeal bench for the matters the town courts cannot settle, and the charge to it has three adverbs: in the fear of the LORD, in faithfulness, and with your whole heart.

Then verse 10, which does something no modern court would say out loud. The judges are to handle cases from their brothers concerning bloodshed and law and commandment and statutes, then you shall warn them, that they may not incur guilt before the LORD and wrath may not come upon you and your brothers.

Two things there. The judge's job includes warning — not only ruling on what has been done but telling people where the edge is before they walk off it. And his own neck is in the case: if he fails to warn, the wrath comes on him too. A bad verdict does not stay with the litigants.

Then the division of jurisdiction, which is remarkably clear-headed for the tenth century before Christ. Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the governor of the house of Judah, in all the king's matters.

Two heads, two kinds of case. Religious questions go up through the priest; crown business goes up through the governor. The same bench hears both and knows which authority it is answering to in each, and the king who set it up has deliberately put half of it beyond his own reach.

The charge ends the way Moses ended his charge to Joshua and David ended his to Solomon. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the upright! Courage is what a judge needs, because the hard cases are hard for one reason: somebody powerful will be unhappy with the answer.

19.theology:
Verses 6 and 7 give a courtroom its theology in two sentences. The bench is not the judge's own — he judges for the LORD, and God stands with him while he does it. And the standard is not a code but a character: there is no injustice with the LORD our God, or partiality or taking bribes. The three things named are the three ways a court actually fails — a wrong verdict, a verdict bent toward the important party, and a verdict bought — and the judges are told what God is like and instructed to match him.

And verse 3 is the shape of God's assessment of his own people. Wrath has gone out, and some good is found, itemised, in the same breath. Neither clause is a qualification of the other, and the man who heard both spent the rest of the chapter working.
19.examples:
The seer who delivered the rebuke was the son of the seer Asa had jailed for delivering one. He knew precisely what the job had cost his father, and he went out to the gate anyway.

Jehoshaphat had sent officials round the towns with the book in his third year. After the rebuke he went himself, from Beersheba to the hills of Ephraim. A man corrected about one thing responded by doing more of the thing he had been right about.

Verse 10 puts the judge's own neck in the case: warn them, so that wrath may not come upon you and your brothers. A bad verdict does not stay with the litigants, and the charge ends by telling the bench it will need courage — because the hard cases are hard for one reason, that somebody powerful will not like the answer.

20.title: The Battle Is Not Yours but God's
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After this the Moabites and Ammonites, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat for battle.<sup>2</sup>Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, "A great multitude is coming against you from Edom, from beyond the sea; and, behold, they are in Hazazon-tamar" (that is, Engedi).<sup>3</sup>Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the LORD, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.<sup>4</sup>And Judah assembled to seek help from the LORD; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the LORD, before the new court,<sup>6</sup>and said, "O LORD, God of our fathers, are you not God in heaven? You rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are power and might, so that none is able to withstand you.<sup>7</sup>Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it forever to the descendants of Abraham your friend?<sup>8</sup>And they have lived in it and have built for you in it a sanctuary for your name, saying,<sup>9</sup>'If disaster comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you— for your name is in this house—and cry out to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.'<sup>10</sup>And now behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, and whom they avoided and did not destroy—<sup>11</sup>behold, they reward us by coming to drive us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit.<sup>12</sup>O our God, will you not execute judgment on them? For we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you."<sup>13</sup>Meanwhile all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.<sup>14</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly.<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Listen, all Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat: Thus says the LORD to you, 'Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's.<sup>16</sup>Tomorrow go down against them.
